Negative Parts:

I do understand the fact that a theory class is supposed to be a lecture-based course rather than a discussion-based course, due to Bilkent's ideology. Nevertheless, a game theory class may be taught with room for discussion by eliminating the time spent on deriving every single equation on the board. Even the best universities in the world teach similar material sometimes through presentations, or pre-handwritten handouts, so that the algebra does not steal from the important part, which is the intuition and results.
2

Bilkent Econ Department may offer a Game Theory course that is also designed to be helpful in other faculties, including engineering and Math. Yet, the course should never put more emphasis on results-based mechanical outcomes and give more attention to its applications in economies, policies, and markets. Deriving a Nash Equilibrium from a 50-line equation sheet and stating that it is the conclusion seems insufficient since it lacks the intuition and application to economics. Again, I understand that the derivation part is crucial. However, the balance between them can be enhanced by alternative methods, such as providing better materials, holding recitation or tutorial sessions, and reducing the time cost of the class. If the Econ department wants to offer this kind of only derivation-based mechanical repetition class, they may consider offering it as "Game Theory for Engineers".
